screens.title: Reshaping Documents with $project and $addFields
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn how two closely related aggregation stages reshape documents in MongoDB. We'll compare $project, which defines a new document shape and can remove fields you don't include, with $addFields, which non-destructively appends or overwrites fields while keeping existing data. You'll see concrete examples that compute names, totals, and year values, and you'll practice a small pipeline that uses $addFields for intermediate calculations followed by $project to shape final output. Understanding the distinction matters because using the wrong stage can either drop fields you still need, or let large documents flow through the pipeline and hurt performance. We will walk through expression operators commonly used inside these stages: arithmetic, string, date, conditional, array, boolean, and comparison operators. By the end you'll be able to decide when to enrich documents, when to trim them, and how to chain these stages safely. A short live-coding style walkthrough will show a products example and a students hands-on activity so you can practice the pattern of compute-then-project.

screens.title: The behavioral difference: $project vs $addFields
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the two stages precisely so you can reason about pipelines. Use $project when you want to define a new document for subsequent stages. $project acts like a selector and a constructor: when you specify included fields, every field not included is removed from the document stream unless you explicitly keep it. That implicit exclusion is powerful when you want minimal documents for performance or to present a final report. A common pitfall is accidentally dropping fields needed later by earlier stages because $project removed them. In contrast, $addFields is additive: it preserves all existing fields by default and only adds or overwrites the fields you list. You can create computed fields or copy nested values to top-level keys without losing the rest of the document. This makes $addFields ideal for intermediate calculations that later stages will use. A useful pattern is to compute helper values with $addFields, then use $project at the end to remove intermediate fields and present a concise output. Remember: if your goal is to reduce payload size early, prefer $project; if you need additional data during processing, choose $addFields. Consider whether you might need original fields later before using $project.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Behavioral difference
Definition
When to replace and when to enrich.
$project — Document replacement
Defines a new top-level document. Unspecified fields are removed unless explicitly included.
$addFields — Non-destructive enrichment
Adds or overwrites fields while keeping all existing fields intact by default.
Common misconception
Using $project early can drop fields you later need. Using $addFields everywhere keeps fields but may carry unnecessary data through the pipeline.
Concrete example
Starting document: name, contact, address, purchases. Use $addFields to compute a purchaseTotal while keeping all fields. Later, use $project to return only name and purchaseTotal for a report.
Key takeaway
Pick $addFields for intermediate computations and $project for final shaping to balance clarity and performance.
Try this: before you use $project, ask whether future stages need any field you might remove.

screens.title: $project syntax and common uses
screens.narratorSegment: Now we examine $project's syntax and how it behaves in common patterns. The $project stage takes a document that describes the outgoing shape of each input document. You can include fields by setting fieldName to 1, exclude fields with 0, but you cannot mix inclusion and exclusion except for the special _id field. You can rename fields by assigning a new key to an existing field path using the dollar prefix, for example newField: "$oldField". You can also create computed fields using expression objects, such as concatenating strings or performing arithmetic. Another powerful use is embedding or de-embedding documents: you can extract a nested object like contact. email directly into a top-level email field, or you can construct a nested object by combining fields under a new key. The most important practical rule is this: if you include any explicit fields, everything else is dropped; so when you want to keep many existing keys it's often safer to use $addFields first. Use $project to minimize document size before a final output or when you want a predictable structure for consumers.

keyIdea.title: $project rules
keyIdea.text: Including fields implicitly excludes others. Use explicit paths and expressions to rename, compute, and embed data into new structures.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › $project syntax
Common $project patterns
  • Include fields: { fieldName: 1 }
  • Exclude fields: { fieldName: 0 } (don't mix with inclusion)
  • Rename: { newName: "$oldName" }
  • Computed fields: expression objects such as { fullName: { $concat: ["$firstName"," ","$lastName"] } }
Concrete example
db.users.aggregate([
  { $project: {
      _id: 0,
      fullName: { $concat: ["$firstName", " ", "$lastName"] },
      email: "$contact.email",
      location: "$address"
    }
  }
])
This $project constructs fullName from two fields, extracts a nested email, and renames address to location. All other original fields are removed because they were not included.
Key Takeaway

$project defines the outgoing document explicitly. Be deliberate about which fields you include to avoid accidental data loss.

screens.title: Example: users collection with fullName, email, and location
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the users example step by step so you internalize what $project does. The starting document contains firstName, lastName, contact with email and phone, and address. The pipeline uses a single $project stage that sets _id to 0 to exclude it, constructs fullName by concatenating firstName and lastName, extracts email from contact. email, and renames address to location. When this $project runs, fields not listed are dropped from the stream, which is why firstName, lastName, and contact. phone vanish in the output; their values are only present in the newly created fields. This pattern is useful when you want a clean response object for an A P I or report. A frequent confusion is thinking $project copies all fields and augments them; instead it creates a new document layout. If you still need the original data elsewhere in the pipeline, compute the new fields with $addFields first and then project only at the end. Try to read the projected output and verify that only the intended keys survive. That discipline prevents accidental loss of important data in later aggregation stages.

screens.title: $addFields: syntax, overwriting, and non-destructive adds
screens.narratorSegment: Now focus on $addFields and its practical role. $addFields takes a document mapping new or existing field names to expressions. When you add a field that already exists, $addFields overwrites that value. When you add a new field, it appears at the top level alongside all original keys. Because it preserves existing fields by default, $addFields is ideal for intermediate calculations you need in later stages, like subtotals or normalized values. A common usage pattern chains $addFields stages to compute values in steps: first compute an orderTotal by multiplying price and quantity, then compute a taxAmount using that newly created orderTotal. Because each $addFields preserves context, the second stage can reference the first stage's new fields. Remember that $addFields changes the document size by adding fields, so if you are sensitive to performance, remove temporary fields with $project at the end. A typical mistake is using $addFields when you intended to prune the document instead; the result will be larger documents flowing through the pipeline. Use $addFields deliberately to keep context while enriching documents. $addFields: syntax, overwriting, and non-destructive adds means $addfields appends or overwrites fields without removing existing keys; use it for intermediate calculations and enrichment.. In practical terms, add intermediate computed fields while preserving document context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › $addFields anatomy
How $addFields works
Provide new keys mapped to expressions. Existing fields remain unchanged unless overwritten. Useful for intermediate values and enriching records used later in the pipeline.
Chaining example
{ $addFields: { orderTotal: { $multiply: ["$price", "$quantity"] } } }
{ $addFields: { taxAmount: { $multiply: ["$orderTotal", 0.08] } } }
Concrete example
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $addFields: { orderTotal: { $multiply: ["$price", "$quantity"] } } },
  { $addFields: { taxAmount: { $multiply: ["$orderTotal", 0.08] } } }
])
The second stage can reference orderTotal created by the first stage. If you need a smaller result later, follow with $project to select only the fields you want.

screens.title: Chaining $addFields then $project
screens.narratorSegment: Here is a common pipeline pattern you will use often: compute intermediate values with $addFields, then finalize the document shape with $project. The pattern has three steps. First, use $addFields to add derived values you will need for grouping, sorting, or further computation. Second, optionally add another $addFields to compute values that depend on earlier derived fields. Third, use $project to remove intermediate fields and return a compact final shape for downstream clients or results. For example, an orders pipeline might compute orderTotal as price times quantity, then compute taxAmount from orderTotal, and finally project only item name, orderTotal, taxAmount, and finalPrice. The benefit is clarity: intermediate fields make subsequent expressions readable and maintainable, while a final project ensures responses are small and predictable. The main misconceptions to avoid are forgetting to project away temporary fields when document size matters, and expecting $project to preserve intermediate fields unless they are explicitly included. Chaining $addFields then $project means compute with $addfields, chain computations if needed, then $project to trim intermediate fields and present final results.. In practical terms, compute intermediate values, then produce a concise final output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Chaining pattern
Pattern: compute then project
A three-step flow to compute intermediate values and finalize output.
Step 1
$addFields for base computation
Compute orderTotal with price*quantity.
Step 2
$addFields for dependent values
Compute taxAmount from orderTotal.
Step 3
$project for final shape
Select only the fields you want to return to clients.
Code pattern
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $addFields: { orderTotal: { $multiply: ["$price", "$quantity"] } } },
  { $addFields: { taxAmount: { $multiply: ["$orderTotal", 0.08] } } },
  { $project: { _id: 0, item: 1, orderTotal: 1, taxAmount: 1, finalPrice: { $add: ["$orderTotal", "$taxAmount"] } } }
])

screens.title: Expression operators used inside $project and $addFields
screens.narratorSegment: Both $project and $addFields accept expressions and share the same pool of operators; knowing which operators serve which tasks will make your pipelines expressive and concise. Arithmetic operators like $add, $subtract, $multiply and $divide compute numeric values for totals, differences, and conversions. String operators such as $concat build a display name from first and last names. Date operators such as $year or $dateToString extract or format components from date fields, useful for reporting by year or month. Conditional operators like $cond and $switch let you branch logic inside a stage, for example to assign grade labels based on numeric values. Array operators like $avg, $size, $map, and $filter let you compute statistics and transform array contents. Boolean operators combine predicates, and comparison operators compare values for conditional logic. A frequent pattern is to use $addFields to compute intermediate numbers with arithmetic and array operators, then use $project with conditional expressions to map those numbers into categories. Remember that expressions can reference newly created fields from previous $addFields stages, enabling readable stepwise computations. Expression operators used inside $project and $addFields means use the right operator family—arithmetic for math, string for concatenation, date for extraction, conditional for branching, array for collection ops—to compute fields inside stages.. screens.title: Hands-on: students pipeline (solution walkthrough)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's solve the students hands-on task step by step. The goal is to add fullName by concatenation, compute averageGrade using an array operator, extract enrollmentYear from enrollmentDate, and finally project only the required fields. First use $addFields to create fullName with $concat and averageGrade with $avg over the grades array. Add enrollmentYear using the $year date operator on enrollmentDate. Because $addFields preserves existing fields, you can chain these expressions and reference created fields if needed. After computing these values, use $project to select only _id, fullName, averageGrade, and enrollmentYear. This pattern yields a small, readable result set suitable for reports. Starter data
{ "_id": 1, "firstName": "Alice", "lastName": "Smith", "grades": [90,85,92], "enrollmentDate": ISODate("2022-09-01T00:00:00Z") }

Solution pipeline

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how two closely related aggregation stages reshape documents in MongoDB. We'll compare $project, which defines a new document shape and can remove fields you don't include, with $addFields, which non-destructively appends or overwrites fields while keeping existing data. You'll see concrete examples that compute names, totals, and year values, and you'll practice a small pipeline that uses $addFields for intermediate calculations followed by $project to shape final output. Understanding the distinction matters because using the wrong stage can either drop fields you still need, or let large documents flow through the pipeline and hurt performance. We will walk through expression operators commonly used inside these stages: arithmetic, string, date, conditional, array, boolean, and comparison operators. By the end you'll be able to decide when to enrich documents, when to trim them, and how to chain these stages safely. A short live-coding style walkthrough will show a products example and a students hands-on activity so you can practice the pattern of compute-then-project.

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to tell the practical difference between $project and $addFields, and apply each where it makes sense. You'll practice reshaping documents with precise field inclusion, exclusion, and renaming, and you'll use $addFields to add computed fields without discarding existing data. The chapter also develops fluency with expression operators so you can compute totals, manipulate strings, extract dates, and work with arrays inside aggregation stages. Finally, you'll learn a common pipeline pattern: compute intermediate values with $addFields and then use $project to present a concise final document. Each objective is paired with a small verification step to confirm competency so you can apply these skills with confidence in pipelines and reports. Learning Objectives means differentiate destructive reshaping ($project) from non-destructive enrichment ($addfields) and use expressions to compute fields.. In practical terms, what you'll be able to do after this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This page maps each objective to a small practice and an assessment idea so you can verify your understanding. For differentiation, you'll explain a pipeline choice for a given scenario and justify why $project or $addFields is better. For shaping with $project, you'll build a stage that renames contact fields and excludes internal IDs. For non-destructive enrichment, you'll add computed totals and retain original item data. For expressions, you'll implement an average calculation and an extraction of a year from an enrollment date. Each practice includes a micro-task and a check: run the pipeline and inspect whether the expected fields exist and hold correct values. These exercises replicate real pipeline patterns: compute intermediate values with $addFields, then reduce to the final shape with $project. Completing these tasks confirms both conceptual understanding and practical skill in everyday aggregation work.

Let's define the two stages precisely so you can reason about pipelines. Use $project when you want to define a new document for subsequent stages. $project acts like a selector and a constructor: when you specify included fields, every field not included is removed from the document stream unless you explicitly keep it. That implicit exclusion is powerful when you want minimal documents for performance or to present a final report. A common pitfall is accidentally dropping fields needed later by earlier stages because $project removed them. In contrast, $addFields is additive: it preserves all existing fields by default and only adds or overwrites the fields you list. You can create computed fields or copy nested values to top-level keys without losing the rest of the document. This makes $addFields ideal for intermediate calculations that later stages will use. A useful pattern is to compute helper values with $addFields, then use $project at the end to remove intermediate fields and present a concise output. Remember: if your goal is to reduce payload size early, prefer $project; if you need additional data during processing, choose $addFields. Consider whether you might need original fields later before using $project.

Now we examine $project's syntax and how it behaves in common patterns. The $project stage takes a document that describes the outgoing shape of each input document. You can include fields by setting fieldName to 1, exclude fields with 0, but you cannot mix inclusion and exclusion except for the special _id field. You can rename fields by assigning a new key to an existing field path using the dollar prefix, for example newField: "$oldField". You can also create computed fields using expression objects, such as concatenating strings or performing arithmetic. Another powerful use is embedding or de-embedding documents: you can extract a nested object like contact. email directly into a top-level email field, or you can construct a nested object by combining fields under a new key. The most important practical rule is this: if you include any explicit fields, everything else is dropped; so when you want to keep many existing keys it's often safer to use $addFields first. Use $project to minimize document size before a final output or when you want a predictable structure for consumers.

Let's walk through the users example step by step so you internalize what $project does. The starting document contains firstName, lastName, contact with email and phone, and address. The pipeline uses a single $project stage that sets _id to 0 to exclude it, constructs fullName by concatenating firstName and lastName, extracts email from contact. email, and renames address to location. When this $project runs, fields not listed are dropped from the stream, which is why firstName, lastName, and contact. phone vanish in the output; their values are only present in the newly created fields. This pattern is useful when you want a clean response object for an A P I or report. A frequent confusion is thinking $project copies all fields and augments them; instead it creates a new document layout. If you still need the original data elsewhere in the pipeline, compute the new fields with $addFields first and then project only at the end. Try to read the projected output and verify that only the intended keys survive. That discipline prevents accidental loss of important data in later aggregation stages.

Now focus on $addFields and its practical role. $addFields takes a document mapping new or existing field names to expressions. When you add a field that already exists, $addFields overwrites that value. When you add a new field, it appears at the top level alongside all original keys. Because it preserves existing fields by default, $addFields is ideal for intermediate calculations you need in later stages, like subtotals or normalized values. A common usage pattern chains $addFields stages to compute values in steps: first compute an orderTotal by multiplying price and quantity, then compute a taxAmount using that newly created orderTotal. Because each $addFields preserves context, the second stage can reference the first stage's new fields.
